title: Dictionary Variables Basics
description: MENTOR-9: "Lists use numbers as labels. But sometimes we need NAMES as labels—like 'captain' or 'status'. That's what dictionaries do: they store key-value pairs."

theory.title: Dictionary Variables: Key-Value Pairs
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 projects a holographic table with two columns: names on the left, values on the right.

MENTOR-9: "Lists work when order matters—first, second, third. But when you need NAMED access, like 'captain' or 'engine_status', you need a DICTIONARY. Keys map to values."

What Are Dictionary Variables?

A dictionary stores key-value pairs—like a lookup table where each key has an associated value:

&{crew}    Create Dictionary    captain=Kirk    engineer=Scott
# Access: ${crew}[captain] → "Kirk"
#         ${crew}[engineer] → "Scott"

Dictionary Syntax

  • Declare/create: &{dict_name}
  • Pass entire dictionary: &{dict_name}
  • Access single value: ${dict_name}[key]

Note the syntax difference:

  • &{} = entire dictionary (multiple key-value pairs)
  • ${} = single value from dictionary (one value)

Creating Dictionaries

Use the Create Dictionary keyword:

&{person}    Create Dictionary    name=Alice    age=30    role=Engineer
&{config}    Create Dictionary    timeout=60    retry=true
&{empty}    Create Dictionary    # Empty dictionary

Syntax: key=value with spaces between pairs.

Accessing Dictionary Values

Access values using keys in square brackets:

&{ship}    Create Dictionary    name=Enterprise    class=Constitution
Log    ${ship}[name]    # Output: Enterprise
Log    ${ship}[class]    # Output: Constitution

Adding/Updating Dictionary Entries

Use Set To Dictionary to add new keys or update existing ones:

&{config}    Create Dictionary    url=example.com
Set To Dictionary    ${config}    port    8080
# Now: {url: example.com, port: 8080}

Set To Dictionary    ${config}    url    newurl.com
# Updated: {url: newurl.com, port: 8080}

Important: When modifying dictionaries, use ${dict} not &{dict}.

Logging Dictionaries

Two ways to log dictionaries:

&{data}    Create Dictionary    x=10    y=20

# Log entire dictionary as key=value pairs
Log    Config: &{data}
# Output: Config: x=10, y=20

# Log as Python dict representation
Log    ${data}
# Output: {'x': '10', 'y': '20'}

Common Dictionary Operations

  • Create Dictionary: Make a new dictionary
  • Set To Dictionary: Add/update key-value pair
  • Get From Dictionary: Retrieve value by key (alternative to ${dict}[key])
  • Remove From Dictionary: Delete key-value pair
  • Get Dictionary Keys: Get list of all keys
  • Get Dictionary Values: Get list of all values
  • Dictionary Should Contain Key: Verify key exists

Why Use Dictionaries?

  • Named access: ${config}[timeout] is clearer than ${config}[3]
  • Structured data: Group related properties together
  • Flexible schema: Add/remove keys dynamically
  • Self-documenting: Keys describe what values represent

Lists vs Dictionaries

FeatureLists (@{})Dictionaries (&{})
Access Numeric index (0, 1, 2) Named key (name, status)
Order Guaranteed order No guaranteed order (Python 3.7+ preserves insertion order)
Use when Sequential items, iteration Related properties, configuration
Example ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] {name: "Alice", age: 30}

Real-World Example

*** Test Cases ***
API Configuration
    &{api_config}    Create Dictionary
    ...    base_url=https://api.example.com
    ...    timeout=30
    ...    retry_count=3
    ...    api_key=abc123
    
    Log    Connecting to: ${api_config}[base_url]
    Log    Timeout: ${api_config}[timeout] seconds
    
    # Update configuration dynamically
    Set To Dictionary    ${api_config}    environment    production
    
    Send API Request    &{api_config}

This shows how dictionaries organize configuration data with meaningful keys.
